title: How long is the projection of a tilted stick?
description: A stick five centimetres long is held above a table with one end three centimetres higher than the other. The board drops both ends straight down, makes a right triangle with the stick as its longest side, and finds the projection. Keeko's doubt is that the projection is two centimetres.
teaching_notes: One idea: the stick, its projection and the height gap form a right triangle, and the stick is the longest side. Watch for students who subtract the lengths instead of the squares.

source: A stick 5 cm long is held above a table so that one end is 3
video_script.why: The child finds the length of a projection by drawing the right triangle of the stick, its projection and the height gap, because the stick is the longest side and the squares take away.
video_script.substitution: stick 5 cm; height gap 3 cm; projection squared = 5 x 5 - 3 x 3 = 25 - 9 = 16; projection = square root of 16 = 4 cm.
video_script.anchor: the stick above the table with both ends dropped straight down, forming a right triangle
video_script.wrong_answer: the stick is five and the gap is three, so the projection is two centimetres
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko takes 5 - 3 = 2 cm; the gap stands upright and the projection lies flat, at a right angle, so the squares take away: 25 - 9 = 16 and the projection is 4 cm, which strikes the doubt.
video_script.payoff_line: The projection is four centimetres, shorter than the stick

final_answer.spoken: four centimetres, shorter than the stick

names.{{NAME_1}}: the theorem used for the shortest path of 40 cm

maths_rules: the projection of an object is made by dropping every place of it straight down onto the plane, at a right angle
the stick, its projection and the height gap make a right triangle; the stick is the longest side
square of the longest side = sum of the squares of the other two
projection = square root of 16 = 4 cm, shorter than the stick
wrong idea: 5 - 3 = 2 takes away the lengths; at a right angle the squares take away
video_script.design: One idea: the stick, its projection and the gap make a right triangle. The stick is held above the table on the stage; both ends drop straight down, and the triangle is drawn in the accent colour.

narration: <bookmark mark='long'/>Step one, name the sides of the right triangle. The stick is the longest side, five centimetres.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>The height gap is the upright side, three centimetres.
<bookmark mark='flat'/>The projection is the flat side that we want.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: square of the longest side = sum of the squares of the other two; projection squared = 5 x 5 - 3 x 3

marks.rule: the rule: square of the longest side = sum of the squares of the other two
marks.rewrite: the rule is rewritten as projection squared = 5 x 5 - 3 x 3

narration: <bookmark mark='rule'/>Step two, the {{NAME_1}} Theorem is about right triangles. It says the square of the longest side is the sum of the squares of the other two.
<bookmark mark='rewrite'/>Here, the square of the projection is the square of five, take away the square of three.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: projection squared = 5 x 5 - 3 x 3 = 25 - 9 = 16; projection = square root of 16

marks.sq: the squares 25 and 9 are written one under the other
marks.root: the words projection = square root of 16 are written

narration: <bookmark mark='sq'/>Step three, five times five is twenty five, and three times three is nine.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Twenty five take away nine is sixteen.
<bookmark mark='root'/>The projection is the square root of sixteen.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 4 cm, shorter than the stick

marks.root: the square root is worked out

narration: <bookmark mark='root'/>The square root of sixteen is four.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>The projection is four centimetres, shorter than the stick.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the stick is five and the gap is three, so the projection is two centimetres.
<bookmark mark='angle'/>The gap stands upright and the projection lies flat, at a right angle.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Sides at a right angle do not take away like that. Their squares do.
